tips.text: Woher kommst du? → Ich komme aus … (not 'Aus Spanien'). Wie alt bist du? → Ich bin … Jahre alt. Match the verb in the question.

examples.de: Hast du Geschwister? – Ja, ich habe einen Bruder.
examples.en: Do you have siblings? – Yes, I have a brother.

examples.de: Wo wohnst du? – Ich wohne in Lyon.
examples.en: Where do you live? – I live in Lyon.

check.q: Woher kommst du? Pick the full-sentence answer to this question.
check.why: The question uses kommst, so you answer with the matching ich komme aus … in a full sentence.

tips.title: Use what this level gave you
tips.text: sein and haben, the -e / -st / -t endings, der/die/das, numbers to 100, colours: the tutor listens for exactly these.

examples.de: Mein Auto ist blau. Ich habe zwei Katzen. Sie sind schwarz.
examples.en: My car is blue. I have two cats. They are black.

examples.de: Mein Bruder ist zwanzig und wohnt in Wien.
examples.en: My brother is twenty and lives in Vienna.

check.why: Meine Katzen are 'they', and sein for sie (plural) is sind.

tips.title: Ask back
tips.text: Und du? / Und Sie? turns an answer into a conversation and buys you a second to think.

examples.de: Ich komme aus Irland. Und du?
examples.en: I'm from Ireland. And you?

examples.de: Ich habe zwei Geschwister. Und Sie?
examples.en: I have two siblings. And you?

check.why: Und du? hands the question back: 'And you?'

remember: Whole sentences only — the score is on the sentence, not the word.
Keep talking through mistakes; the corrections come at the end.
help.exam: A short conversation about yourself and your family is the heart of the A1 speaking exam — and of every first chat with a neighbour.
help.hook: Hold a five-minute chat about yourself in German: your name, home, family, and the numbers and colours around you.

writing.topic: Introduce yourself in writing, the way you would on a profile or a form: your name, how old you are, where you come from, where you live now, what you do, and one thing you like.
practisePoints: say your name with heißen or sein
say where you come from with kommen aus and where you live with wohnen in
write every noun with a capital letter
keep the verb in second place in each sentence
scoringCriteria: all six pieces of information are there
the verb endings match the subject

help.hook: Write six true sentences about yourself, and have them corrected one by one.
help.intro: Your first piece of real German writing. Six short sentences are enough: your name, your age, where you are from, where you live, what you do, and one thing you like. You write them here in the box, and the app builds a correction request that carries your own text to your AI, which corrects what you actually wrote. Aim for 120 to 300 characters. Do not reach for words you have not met yet. A short, correct text scores better than an ambitious one full of guesses, and that is true at every level of this course.

tips.title: The verb is always the second idea
tips.text: German puts the conjugated verb in second position, whatever comes first. If you open with the subject, the verb follows it. If you open with something else, the verb still comes second and the subject moves behind it.

examples.de: Ich wohne jetzt in Berlin.
examples.en: I live in Berlin now.

examples.de: Jetzt wohne ich in Berlin.
examples.en: Now I live in Berlin.

check.why: After an opening word the verb comes straight away, then the subject.

tips.trap: „Jetzt ich wohne in Berlin“ is the commonest first mistake: the verb has been pushed to third place.

tips.title: heißen, sein, kommen, wohnen
tips.text: Four verbs carry a self-introduction. ich heiße (I am called), ich bin (I am), ich komme aus (I come from), ich wohne in (I live in). aus is for the country or town you are from; in is for where you live now.

examples.de: Ich heiße Ana und ich bin 26 Jahre alt.
examples.en: My name is Ana and I am 26.

examples.de: Ich komme aus Spanien und wohne in Hamburg.
examples.en: I am from Spain and live in Hamburg.

check.why: aus is the preposition for the country you come from.

tips.title: Every noun gets a capital letter
tips.text: German writes every noun with a capital letter, wherever it stands in the sentence: Jahre, Spanien, Deutsch, Familie, Bruder. It is the thing a corrector notices first in a written text, and it costs nothing to get right.

examples.de: Ich lerne Deutsch und ich habe einen Bruder.
examples.en: I am learning German and I have a brother.

examples.de: Meine Familie wohnt in Madrid.
examples.en: My family lives in Madrid.

check.why: Schwester is a noun, so it is capitalised, and the sentence starts with a capital too.

remember: The verb is the second idea, always.
ich heiße, ich bin, ich komme aus, ich wohne in.
Every noun takes a capital letter.
Six true sentences beat twelve guessed ones.
help.exam: Writing a few lines about yourself is the first written task of the A1 certificate, and the first thing anyone asks you in German.

mistakes.why: The verb keeps second place; the subject moves behind it.
aus for the country you come from.
German has an age with sein, not haben.
The name of a language is a noun.

vocab.en: gladly, used to say you like doing something

help.intro: Wie schreibt man das? — how do you spell that? — is a question you will hear on your first day in any German office, and on the phone, at the doctor's and at every hotel desk you will be asked to spell your name. The German alphabet has the same 26 letters as English plus ä, ö, ü and ß, but many letters have different names, and the ones that differ are exactly the ones English speakers mix up: E is said 'ay' and I is said 'ee' (the other way round from what you expect), J is Jot, V is Vau (said 'fow'), W is We (said 'vay'), Z is Zett ('tset') and Y is Ypsilon. Germans spell with a few fixed helpers: Doppel-L for ll, A-Umlaut for ä, Eszett or scharfes S for ß. This quiz asks for the names of the tricky letters, then gives you names spelt out letter by letter and asks you to write the word.

tips.title: E is "ay", I is "ee"
tips.text: The two vowels English speakers swap: E sounds like English 'ay' in 'day', I like 'ee' in 'see'. A is 'ah', O is 'oh', U is 'oo'.

examples.de: Wie heißen Sie? – Meier. Em – E – I – E – Er.
examples.en: What's your name? – Meier. M – 'ay' – 'ee' – 'ay' – R.

examples.de: Lisa: El – I – Es – A.
examples.en: Lisa: L – 'ee' – S – 'ah'.

tips.trap: When a German spells 'E – I' you hear 'ay – ee'. Write E first, then I.

check.q: Someone spelling a word says 'ee'. Which letter is it?
check.why: In German the letter I sounds like English 'ee', while E sounds like 'ay'.

tips.title: The letters with surprising names
tips.text: J = Jot, V = Vau, W = We, Y = Ypsilon, Z = Zett, Q = Ku, C = Ce (said "tsay"), H = Ha. Say them aloud until they are as automatic as A, B, C.

examples.de: Jot – A – En: Jan
examples.en: J – A – N: Jan

examples.de: Vau – A – Te – E – Er: Vater
examples.en: V – A – T – E – R: Vater

check.q: What is the German name of the letter W?
check.why: W is We (said 'vay'). Vau is the name of V, and Doppel-U is not used.

tips.title: Spelling helpers
tips.text: Two identical letters: Doppel- (Doppel-L, Doppel-S). Umlauts: A-Umlaut, O-Umlaut, U-Umlaut. ß: Eszett or scharfes S. Capital or small: groß / klein.

examples.de: Müller: Em – U-Umlaut – Doppel-El – E – Er.
examples.en: Müller: M – Ü – double L – E – R.

examples.de: Straße schreibt man mit Eszett.
examples.en: Straße is written with ß.

check.q: What do you call ß when you spell a word?
check.why: ß is Eszett (or scharfes S). Doppel-S means two separate s letters, as in Wasser.

tips.title: The front-desk script
tips.text: Wie ist Ihr Name? – … Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren? – Gern: … Practise your own name and your street until you can spell them without stopping.

examples.de: Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?
examples.en: Could you spell that, please?

examples.de: Wie schreibt man das? – Mit Ha am Ende.
examples.en: How do you write that? – With an H at the end.

check.q: You want a name spelt out letter by letter: Können Sie das bitte ____?
check.why: buchstabieren means to spell aloud, letter by letter (from Buchstabe, letter).

remember: E = 'ay', I = 'ee' — the swap that causes most spelling mistakes.
J Jot, V Vau, W We, Z Zett: four letters, four names to learn by heart.

context.de: Wie ist Ihr Name, bitte? – Weber. – Können Sie das buchstabieren? – We – E – Be – E – Er. – Danke. Und Ihr Vorname? – Jana: Jot – A – En – A.
context.en: What's your name, please? – Weber. – Could you spell that? – W – E – B – E – R. – Thanks. And your first name? – Jana: J – A – N – A.

mistakes.wrong: Meier spelt 'M – I – E – I – R'
mistakes.why: E is said 'ay' and I 'ee' — English speakers hear 'ee' and write I.
German W is We; the sound is also how the letter is said in words: Wien, Wasser.
German Z is always ts — in its name too.

help.hook: Wie schreibt man das? Master the dozen letter names that differ from English and you can spell your name anywhere.

help.intro: Rents, prices of bikes and phones, distances, the year you were born: from here on the numbers get long, and German writes them as one word — 650 is sechshundertfünfzig, 1.200 is tausendzweihundert. The good news is that nothing new is hidden inside them. You say the hundreds, then the last two digits exactly as you learnt them, with the unit first: 385 = dreihundert-fünfundachtzig. Thousands work the same way: 8.500 = achttausend-fünfhundert. Two things are different from English. First, German marks thousands with a full stop and decimals with a comma: 1.200 means twelve hundred, 1,20 means one point two. Second, years before 2000 are said in hundreds: 1998 is neunzehnhundertachtundneunzig, never 'tausendneunhundert…'; from 2000 on you say zweitausend: 2020 = zweitausendzwanzig.

tips.title: Hundreds + the number you already know
tips.text: Say how many hundreds, then the last two digits the German way (unit + und + ten). All of it is one word; ein before hundert and tausend is optional.

examples.de: Die Wohnung kostet sechshundertfünfzig Euro.
examples.en: The flat costs 650 euros.

examples.de: Das Buch hat vierhundertsechzehn Seiten.
examples.en: The book has 416 pages.

tips.trap: Do not insert spaces or an extra und after hundert: sechshundertfünfzig, not "sechshundert und fünfzig".

check.why: Say the hundreds, then the last two digits, all as one word with no extra und after hundert.

tips.title: Thousands: the full stop is not a decimal point
tips.text: 1.200 = tausendzweihundert (also zwölfhundert). 8.500 = achttausendfünfhundert. 20.000 = zwanzigtausend. A comma is the decimal point: 1,5 Kilo = one and a half kilos.

examples.de: Die Halle hat tausendzweihundert Plätze.
examples.en: The hall has 1,200 seats.

examples.de: Die Stadt hat zwanzigtausend Einwohner.
examples.en: The town has 20,000 inhabitants.

tips.trap: In English 1.200 is 'one point two'. In German it is twelve hundred.

check.q: A German sign says: 2.500 Einwohner. How many people live there?
check.why: In German the full stop marks thousands: 2.500 = zweitausendfünfhundert. The decimal point is a comma.

tips.title: Years: hundreds before 2000, zweitausend after
tips.text: 1965 = neunzehnhundertfünfundsechzig. 1998 = neunzehnhundertachtundneunzig. 2020 = zweitausendzwanzig. And a year stands alone: Ich bin 1998 geboren — no in.

examples.de: Mein Vater ist neunzehnhundertfünfundsechzig geboren.
examples.en: My father was born in 1965.

examples.de: Meine Tochter ist zweitausendzwanzig geboren.
examples.en: My daughter was born in 2020.

check.why: Years before 2000 are said in hundreds (neunzehnhundert…), and the year stands alone without in.

tips.title: Read from the left, flip the last two
tips.text: Take 585: fünfhundert (left) + fünfundachtzig (flip the 8 and the 5). Only the last pair is ever flipped.

examples.de: 585 → fünfhundert + fünfundachtzig
199 → hundert + neunundneunzig

check.why: Read the hundreds from the left (dreihundert), then flip only the last pair: 76 = sechsundsiebzig.

tips.title: Ordinal numbers: -te up to 19, -ste from 20
tips.text: Dates and rankings use ordinals, written with a full stop: der 1. Mai = der erste Mai. Add -te to the numbers 2 to 19 (zweite, vierte, zehnte, neunzehnte) and -ste from 20 upwards (zwanzigste, dreißigste, hundertste). Four are irregular: erste, dritte, siebte, achte (only one t).

examples.de: Heute ist der erste Mai.
examples.en: Today is the first of May.

examples.de: Morgen ist der dritte Juni.
examples.en: Tomorrow is the third of June.

examples.de: Der einunddreißigste Dezember ist Silvester.
examples.en: The thirty-first of December is New Year’s Eve.

tips.trap: The full stop after the figure is the ordinal mark: 3. Juni reads dritte Juni, never drei Juni.

check.why: From 20 on the ending is -ste.

remember: One number, one word: sechshundertfünfzig, tausendzweihundert.
Years before 2000 in hundreds (neunzehnhundert…), after 2000 with zweitausend.
Ordinals: -te to 19, -ste from 20; erste, dritte, siebte, achte are irregular. 3. Juni = dritte Juni.

context.de: Die Wohnung hat zwei Zimmer und kostet neunhundertachtzig Euro im Monat. Das Haus ist alt – es ist von neunzehnhundertzwölf. Bis zur Arbeit sind es nur zwölf Kilometer, und das Fahrrad kostet hundertneunundneunzig Euro.
context.en: The flat has two rooms and costs 980 euros a month. The house is old – it is from 1912. It is only twelve kilometres to work, and the bike costs 199 euros.

mistakes.why: The whole number is one word, and there is no und after hundert.
Years before 2000 are said in hundreds.
The full stop groups thousands; the comma is the decimal point.

help.hook: Rent, bikes, birth years: big German numbers are just the small ones you know, glued into one long word.

help.intro: Every word this module's exercises use, on one deck of flashcards: the nouns from the article and plural drills, the numbers, the family, the colours, the countries and the verbs. A noun is learnt with its article or not at all, so the write mode only counts "die Stelle", never "Stelle" on its own. Three ways to work through the deck: write the German, choose it from four options, or flip the card and rate yourself honestly. A word you miss comes back later in the same run, and stays in your "Weak words" list until you get it right three times in a row.

tips.title: Article first, always
tips.text: German nouns come in three genders and the article is the only reliable clue. Say der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch as one word each; a bare noun is only half a word.

examples.de: der Tisch, die Tische
examples.en: the table, the tables

examples.de: die Lampe, die Lampen
examples.en: the lamp, the lamps

examples.de: das Buch, die Bücher
examples.en: the book, the books

check.q: You are learning the word for “chair”. What should you memorise?
check.why: The article is the only reliable clue to the gender, so the noun and its article are learnt as one word.

visual.caption: Say the article every time you say the word, and it sticks.

tips.title: Learn the plural with the noun
tips.text: The plural is shown after every correct answer. Read it aloud once: the pattern (-e, -en, -s, -er, umlaut) is what you are memorising, not just the word.

examples.de: der Apfel, die Äpfel
examples.en: the apple, the apples

examples.de: das Kind, die Kinder
examples.en: the child, the children

check.why: Stuhl takes the umlaut + -e pattern: die Stühle. Saying the plural aloud with the noun is how the pattern sticks.

tips.title: Names take no article
tips.text: Countries, cities and letters are capitalised like nouns but stand alone: Berlin, Spanien, Japan. The exceptions with an article are die Schweiz, die Türkei, die USA.

examples.de: Ich komme aus Spanien.
examples.en: I come from Spain.

examples.de: Ich komme aus der Schweiz.
examples.en: I come from Switzerland.

check.why: Country and city names stand alone without an article; only a few like die Schweiz and die Türkei keep one.

remember: Never say a noun without its article — not even in your head.
Miss a word? It comes back in the same run. Get it right three times and it leaves the weak list.
help.hook: A German noun without its article is only half a word — learn der, die or das and the plural with it, every time.
A cosy living room full of everyday things: tap each one in the picture, then give it its article.
help.intro: A picture hunt instead of a deck: one cosy, slightly cluttered living room with 32 things to find in it, the everyday words you need first — der Tisch, die Lampe, das Sofa, the cat asleep on the cushions and the dog on the rug. The prompt asks Wo ist der Sessel? and you tap it in the picture. Each find shows its label, coloured by its gender, then leaves a small tick in that colour, so you can see what you have already found. Once you have passed a run, the hunt turns harder: the prompt hides the article (Wo ist ___ Sessel?), and after the find you choose der, die or das yourself. A tap on bare wall costs nothing; a tap on the wrong object tells you what you hit and you keep looking, and after three misses the right one is shown. No object is asked twice in the same run.

tips.title: Many nouns in -e are die
tips.text: Look at how many words in this room end in -e: die Lampe, die Tasse, die Kerze, die Vase, die Katze, die Pflanze, die Gitarre. Most German nouns ending in -e are feminine, so when you meet a new one, guess die first.

examples.de: die Kerze, Plural: -n
examples.en: candle

examples.de: die Gitarre, Plural: -n
examples.en: guitar

check.why: Tasse ends in -e, and most nouns in -e are feminine: die Tasse.

tips.title: Die Brille is one thing
tips.text: English says glasses, a plural, but German says die Brille, one object. And das Glas is something else: the glass of water on the table. Don’t mix them up.

examples.de: die Brille
examples.en: (a pair of) glasses

examples.de: das Glas, Plural: Gläser
examples.en: drinking glass

check.q: Which one do you put on your nose?
check.why: Die Brille is the pair of glasses; das Glas is for drinking.

tips.title: International words in -o are often das
tips.text: Words German took from other languages and that end in -o are usually neuter: das Radio, das Auto, das Kino. das Sofa is neuter too, but most words in -a are die (die Pizza, die Kamera). Picture them all parked together in one das-garage.

examples.de: das Sofa, Plural: -s
examples.en: sofa

examples.de: das Radio, Plural: -s
examples.en: radio

check.why: Auto ends in -o, like Radio: das Auto.

remember: Most nouns ending in -e are die: die Lampe, die Tasse, die Katze.
Die Brille is singular in German: one pair of glasses.
A compound takes the article of its last part: der Regen + der Schirm → der Regenschirm.

quiz.title: Suchbild: Das Wohnzimmer
quiz.sceneAlt: A cosy living room: a window with a curtain, a floor lamp, a guitar and an armchair on the left, a picture, a clock and wall shelves with a vase, a radio and a telephone on the back wall, a television on a cabinet, a sofa with a cat, a coffee table on a round rug, a dog and a ball on the floor, and by the door an umbrella, a plant and a basket of wool.

help.hook: An empty classroom after the bell: tap each thing you find, then give it its article.
help.intro: A picture hunt instead of a deck: one empty, slightly messy classroom with 32 things to find in it, the words of a school day — die Tafel, der Bleistift, das Heft, the fish tank by the wall and the piano in the corner. The prompt asks Wo ist das Lineal? and you tap it in the picture. Each find shows its label, coloured by its gender, then leaves a small tick in that colour, so you can see what you have already found. Once you have passed a run, the hunt turns harder: the prompt hides the article (Wo ist ___ Lineal?), and after the find you choose der, die or das yourself. A tap on bare wall costs nothing; a tap on the wrong object tells you what you hit and you keep looking, and after three misses the right one is shown. No object is asked twice in the same run.

tips.title: Compounds in the classroom: the last part decides
tips.text: Many classroom words are two words glued together, and the last part decides the article. Papier + Korb: der Korb, so der Papierkorb. Land + Karte: die Karte, so die Landkarte. Hand + Tuch: das Tuch, so das Handtuch.

examples.de: der Bleistift, Plural: -e
examples.en: pencil (der Stift)

examples.de: die Brotdose, Plural: -n
examples.en: lunch box (die Dose)

check.q: ____ Waschbecken ist links an der Wand.
check.why: The last part is das Becken, so the whole word is das Waschbecken.

tips.title: Machines in -er are der
tips.text: A thing that does a job and ends in -er is usually masculine: der Computer, der Drucker, der Taschenrechner. The -er here is not a plural, it is part of the word.

examples.de: der Drucker, Plural: -
examples.en: printer

examples.de: der Taschenrechner, Plural: -
examples.en: calculator

check.why: Computer ends in -er like Drucker: der Computer.

tips.title: -chen is always das
tips.text: A noun ending in -chen is always neuter, whatever it means: das Mäppchen, the little pencil case. Think of -chen as a small green das sticker on anything little.

examples.de: das Mäppchen, Plural: -
examples.en: pencil case

examples.de: das Brötchen, Plural: -
examples.en: bread roll

check.why: Every noun ending in -chen is neuter: das Mäppchen.

remember: The last part of a compound sets the article: der Korb → der Papierkorb.
Machines in -er are der: der Computer, der Drucker.
-chen is always das: das Mäppchen.

quiz.title: Suchbild: Das Klassenzimmer
quiz.sceneAlt: An empty classroom: a chalkboard, a world map and a coat hook with a jacket on the back wall, a sink, a towel, a fish tank and a stool on the left, a piano with a woolly hat on the right, a teacher’s desk with a computer, a globe and a printer, and in front a school desk covered with an exercise book, paper, a ruler, a pencil, a pencil case, scissors, a calculator, a lunch box, a banana and a bottle.

vocab.example: Hamburg ist eine Stadt im Norden.
Der Hafen ist das Herz von Hamburg.
Jedes Jahr kommen etwa achttausend Schiffe.
In Hamburg wohnen fast zwei Millionen Menschen.

quiz.title: Lesen: Hamburg in Zahlen

help.intro: A short text of about 120 words with real facts about Hamburg, told in numbers: how many people live there, how many bridges the city has (more than Venice and Amsterdam together), how old the harbour is and what the river is called. All numbers are real and were checked. You need only what you have learnt: numbers up to a million written as words, Hamburg hat / Hamburg ist, and the question words Wie viele? (how many), Wie alt? (how old), Wo? (where). Read the text once for the gist, then take each question and find the number it asks for.

tips.title: Big numbers in words
tips.text: Hundred = hundert, thousand = tausend, million = eine Million (plural: zwei Millionen). German writes a number as one long word up to a million: zweitausendfünfhundert (2,500). Years are read in hundreds: 1189 = elfhundertneunundachtzig. Watch the order in two-digit numbers: 89 = neunundachtzig, nine-and-eighty.

examples.de: Hamburg hat fast zwei Millionen Einwohner.
examples.en: Hamburg has almost two million inhabitants.

examples.de: Die Stadt hat etwa zweitausendfünfhundert Brücken.
examples.en: The city has about two thousand five hundred bridges.

check.why: neun-und-achtzig = nine and eighty = 89. German says the ones before the tens.

tips.title: Wie viele? Wie alt? Wo?
tips.text: Wie viele Brücken hat Hamburg? asks for a number of things. Wie alt ist der Hafen? asks for an age. Wo liegt Hamburg? asks for a place and gets an answer with in or an: in Norddeutschland, an der Elbe. Find the question word first, then hunt for that kind of answer in the text.

examples.de: Wo liegt Hamburg? Hamburg liegt im Norden von Deutschland, an der Elbe.
examples.en: Where is Hamburg? Hamburg lies in the north of Germany, on the Elbe.

examples.de: Wie alt ist der Hafen? Der Hafen ist über achthundert Jahre alt.
examples.en: How old is the harbour? The harbour is over eight hundred years old.

check.q: Which question asks for a place?
check.why: Wo = where. Wie viele asks for a number, wie alt for an age.

remember: hundert, tausend, eine Million / zwei Millionen; ones before tens: neunundachtzig = 89.
Wo? = place (in, an), Wie viele? = how many, Wie alt? = how old.
help.exam: Short factual texts with numbers and multiple-choice questions are a typical reading task at this level, and exactly what a city guide or a poster looks like.
help.hook: Almost two million people, two and a half thousand bridges, a harbour older than eight hundred years. Read Hamburg in numbers.

quiz.passage:
Hamburg ist eine Stadt im Norden von Deutschland. Die Stadt liegt an der Elbe. Die Elbe ist ein Fluss. Er ist über tausend Kilometer lang und kommt aus Tschechien.

In Hamburg wohnen fast zwei Millionen Menschen. Hamburg ist die zweitgrößte Stadt in Deutschland. Nur Berlin ist größer.

Hamburg hat sehr viel Wasser: die Elbe, die Alster und viele Kanäle. Darum hat die Stadt auch sehr viele Brücken: etwa zweitausendfünfhundert! Das sind mehr Brücken als in Venedig und Amsterdam zusammen.

Der Hafen ist das Herz von Hamburg. Er ist sehr alt: Der Hafen hat Geburtstag am 7. Mai 1189. Er ist also über achthundert Jahre alt. Heute ist der Hamburger Hafen der größte Hafen in Deutschland. Jedes Jahr kommen etwa achttausend Schiffe.

Hamburg hat auch ein berühmtes Konzerthaus: die Elbphilharmonie. Sie ist 110 Meter hoch und steht direkt am Wasser. Von oben sieht man den Hafen, die Elbe und die ganze Stadt.
quiz.passageTranslation:
Hamburg is a city in the north of Germany. The city lies on the Elbe. The Elbe is a river. It is over a thousand kilometres long and comes from the Czech Republic.

Almost two million people live in Hamburg. Hamburg is the second-largest city in Germany. Only Berlin is bigger.

Hamburg has a lot of water: the Elbe, the Alster and many canals. That is why the city also has very many bridges: about two thousand five hundred! That is more bridges than in Venice and Amsterdam together.

The harbour is the heart of Hamburg. It is very old: the harbour has its birthday on 7 May 1189. So it is over eight hundred years old. Today the port of Hamburg is the biggest port in Germany. Every year about eight thousand ships come.

Hamburg also has a famous concert hall: the Elbphilharmonie. It is 110 metres high and stands right by the water. From the top you see the harbour, the Elbe and the whole city.

vocab.example: Müller ist der häufigste Familienname in Deutschland.
Vor siebenhundert Jahren haben die Menschen nur einen Vornamen.
Der Müller arbeitet in der Mühle.
In einem Dorf gibt es zwei Männer mit dem Namen Hans.

quiz.title: Lesen: Warum so viele Müller?

help.intro: A short text of about 130 words about German family names: Müller is the most common one, and it simply means miller, the man who makes flour. Schmidt is the smith, Schneider the tailor, Fischer the fisherman, Weber the weaver, Meyer the farm manager, Bäcker the baker. Most German surnames are old job titles, and the text explains why, with real numbers. You need what you have just learnt: job words and their feminine forms with -in (der Bäcker, die Bäckerin), simple compounds (Familienname = Familie + Name) and the verbs heißen, sein and machen. The questions ask what a name means and how many people carry it.

tips.title: Names that are jobs
tips.text: Müller = miller (Mühle = mill, Mehl = flour). Schmidt / Schmitt / Schmid = smith. Schneider = tailor (schneiden = to cut). Fischer = fisherman. Weber = weaver. Bäcker = baker. Koch = cook. Many German families got their name from the job of a man about seven hundred years ago. The job word is masculine; the woman gets -in: der Müller, die Müllerin; der Bäcker, die Bäckerin.

examples.de: Der Müller macht Mehl. Frau Müller ist aber Lehrerin.
examples.en: The miller makes flour. Ms Müller, however, is a teacher.

examples.de: Herr Fischer ist kein Fischer. Er ist Arzt.
examples.en: Mr Fischer is not a fisherman. He is a doctor.

check.q: What does the name Schneider mean?
check.why: schneiden = to cut; the Schneider cuts cloth and makes clothes.

tips.title: Words built from two words
tips.text: German glues words together. The last part says what it is; the first part says which kind: Familienname = Familie + Name (family name), Vorname = vor + Name (first name), Hausnummer = Haus + Nummer. The last word gives the article: der Name, so der Familienname; die Nummer, so die Hausnummer.

examples.de: Mein Vorname ist Anna, mein Familienname ist Müller.
examples.en: My first name is Anna, my family name is Müller.

examples.de: Der Name ist alt, aber die Berufe sind neu.
examples.en: The name is old, but the jobs are new.

check.q: Familienname: which part gives the article?
check.why: The last part of a compound decides the article.

remember: Müller, Schmidt, Schneider, Fischer, Weber, Bäcker: old jobs that became names.
Compound = last part gives the meaning and the article: der Familienname, die Hausnummer.
help.exam: Short texts about names, jobs and families with multiple-choice questions are a typical reading task at this level.
help.hook: Why do so many Germans have the same name, and what does it mean? Read the story behind Müller, Schmidt and Schneider.

quiz.passage:
In Deutschland heißen sehr viele Menschen Müller. Mehr als siebenhunderttausend! Müller ist der häufigste Familienname in Deutschland. Auf Platz zwei steht Schmidt, auf Platz drei Schneider. Dann kommen Fischer, Weber und Meyer.

Warum? Die Namen sind alt. Vor etwa siebenhundert Jahren haben die Menschen nur einen Vornamen: Hans, Peter, Anna. Aber in einem Dorf gibt es zwei oder drei Männer mit dem Namen Hans. Was macht man? Man sagt: Hans, der Müller. Hans, der Schmied. Hans, der Fischer. Der Beruf wird der Name.

Der Müller arbeitet in der Mühle und macht Mehl. Der Schmied macht Dinge aus Eisen. Der Schneider macht Kleidung. Der Weber macht Stoff. Der Fischer fängt Fische. Der Bäcker backt Brot.

Heute ist Herr Müller vielleicht Arzt, und Frau Fischer ist Lehrerin. Der Name ist alt, aber der Beruf ist neu.
quiz.passageTranslation:
In Germany very many people are called Müller. More than seven hundred thousand! Müller is the most common family name in Germany. In second place is Schmidt, in third Schneider. Then come Fischer, Weber and Meyer.

Why? The names are old. About seven hundred years ago people have only a first name: Hans, Peter, Anna. But in a village there are two or three men with the name Hans. What do you do? You say: Hans the miller. Hans the smith. Hans the fisherman. The job becomes the name.

The miller works in the mill and makes flour. The smith makes things from iron. The tailor makes clothes. The weaver makes cloth. The fisherman catches fish. The baker bakes bread.

Today Mr Müller is perhaps a doctor, and Ms Fischer is a teacher. The name is old, but the job is new.

vocab.example: Deutsch spricht man in vier Ländern.
Liechtenstein liegt zwischen der Schweiz und Österreich.

quiz.title: Lesen: Vier Länder, eine Sprache

help.intro: A short text of about 130 words about the countries where German is spoken: Germany, Austria, Switzerland and little Liechtenstein, plus a surprise about Switzerland, which has four national languages and no language called Swiss. All facts are real and were checked. You need what you have just learnt: country names (most without article, but die Schweiz), the verbs sprechen, wohnen, kommen aus and liegen, and the languages Deutsch, Französisch, Italienisch. Read for the gist first, then answer each question from one sentence.

tips.title: Countries with and without an article
tips.text: Most countries have no article: Deutschland, Österreich, Liechtenstein, Frankreich, Italien. A few are feminine and take die: die Schweiz, die Türkei, die Ukraine. After aus and in, die becomes der: aus der Schweiz, in der Schweiz; but aus Österreich, in Österreich. The language is usually the country word with -isch: Französisch, Italienisch; Deutsch has no -isch.

examples.de: Lukas kommt aus der Schweiz und wohnt jetzt in Österreich.
examples.en: Lukas comes from Switzerland and now lives in Austria.

examples.de: In Liechtenstein spricht man Deutsch, in Genf Französisch.
examples.en: In Liechtenstein people speak German, in Geneva French.

check.why: Schweiz takes die; after aus it becomes der.

rows.b: aus der Schweiz, in der Schweiz

tips.title: man = people in general
tips.text: In der Schweiz spricht man vier Sprachen: man means people, one, you in general. It takes the er/sie/es form of the verb: man spricht, man sagt, man wohnt. Very common in texts about countries and customs.

examples.de: In Österreich sagt man Grüß Gott, in Hamburg sagt man Moin.
examples.en: In Austria people say Grüß Gott, in Hamburg people say Moin.

examples.de: Wie sagt man danke auf Französisch? Merci.
examples.en: How do you say thank you in French? Merci.

check.q: In der Schweiz ____ man Deutsch, Französisch, Italienisch und Rätoromanisch.
check.why: man takes the er/sie/es form: man spricht.

remember: die Schweiz: aus der Schweiz, in der Schweiz; other countries without article.
man spricht / man sagt = people speak / people say.
help.exam: Short factual texts about countries and languages with multiple-choice questions are a typical reading task at this level.
help.hook: Four countries speak German, and one of them has four languages but no language of its own. Read which, and who is the smallest.

quiz.passage:
Deutsch spricht man in vier Ländern in Europa: in Deutschland, in Österreich, in der Schweiz und in Liechtenstein.

Deutschland ist groß. Hier wohnen etwa vierundachtzig Millionen Menschen. Die Hauptstadt ist Berlin. Österreich ist kleiner. Dort wohnen etwa neun Millionen Menschen. Die Hauptstadt ist Wien.

Die Schweiz ist besonders. Sie hat vier Sprachen: Deutsch, Französisch, Italienisch und Rätoromanisch. Etwa sechzig Prozent sprechen Deutsch. In Genf spricht man Französisch, in Lugano Italienisch. Eine Sprache „Schweizerisch“ gibt es nicht! Die Hauptstadt ist Bern, aber die größte Stadt ist Zürich.

Liechtenstein ist sehr klein. Es liegt zwischen der Schweiz und Österreich. Dort wohnen nur vierzigtausend Menschen. Das Land hat keinen Flughafen und keine Autobahn. Die Hauptstadt heißt Vaduz.

In Basel gibt es einen besonderen Ort: das Dreiländereck. Hier treffen sich Deutschland, Frankreich und die Schweiz. Man steht in einem Land und sieht zwei andere.
quiz.passageTranslation:
German is spoken in four countries in Europe: in Germany, in Austria, in Switzerland and in Liechtenstein.

Germany is big. About eighty-four million people live here. The capital is Berlin. Austria is smaller. About nine million people live there. The capital is Vienna.

Switzerland is special. It has four languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. About sixty per cent speak German. In Geneva people speak French, in Lugano Italian. A language called 'Swiss' does not exist! The capital is Bern, but the biggest city is Zurich.

Liechtenstein is very small. It lies between Switzerland and Austria. Only forty thousand people live there. The country has no airport and no motorway. The capital is called Vaduz.

In Basel there is a special place: the three-country corner. Here Germany, France and Switzerland meet. You stand in one country and see two others.

vocab.example: Die Flagge von Deutschland hat drei Streifen.
Die Flagge der Schweiz ist rot mit einem weißen Kreuz.
Die Geschichte sagt: Ein Herzog kämpft im Jahr 1191.
Nur der Gürtel in der Mitte bleibt weiß.
Sie ist eine der ältesten Flaggen der Welt.

quiz.title: Lesen: Drei Flaggen, drei Geschichten

help.intro: A short text of about 130 words about the flags of Germany, Austria and Switzerland: which colours they have, how old they are, and two surprises: the Austrian flag is one of the oldest in the world, and the Swiss flag is square, which only one other flag in the world is. All facts are real and were checked. You need what you have just learnt: the colours (schwarz, rot, gold, weiß), the articles in the nominative (die Flagge, das Kreuz, der Streifen) and the plural of nouns (die Flaggen, die Farben, die Streifen). Read the text once for the gist, then look for one colour or one number per question.

tips.title: Colours as adjectives after sein
tips.text: After ist / sind the colour has no ending: Die Flagge ist rot. Das Kreuz ist weiß. Die Streifen sind schwarz, rot und gold. Colour words are written small, except in a name: das Rote Kreuz. Gold is a colour here (not gelb): Schwarz-Rot-Gold is the German flag's name.

examples.de: Die deutsche Flagge ist schwarz, rot und gold.
examples.en: The German flag is black, red and gold.

examples.de: Das Kreuz ist weiß, die Flagge ist rot.
examples.en: The cross is white, the flag is red.

check.why: After ist the colour has no ending and is written small.

tips.title: Plurals you meet here
tips.text: die Flagge → die Flaggen (-n), die Farbe → die Farben, der Streifen → die Streifen (no change), das Land → die Länder (¨-er), das Kreuz → die Kreuze (-e), das Jahr → die Jahre. In the plural every noun takes die. Watch for the number in front: drei Streifen, zwei Farben, achthundert Jahre.

examples.de: Die Flagge hat drei Streifen und drei Farben.
examples.en: The flag has three stripes and three colours.

examples.de: Die Flagge ist über achthundert Jahre alt.
examples.en: The flag is over eight hundred years old.

check.q: What is the plural of das Land?
check.why: Land takes umlaut + -er: Länder. Plural article is always die.

remember: Colours after ist/sind have no ending: Die Flagge ist rot und weiß.
Plural always die: die Flaggen, die Farben, die Streifen, die Länder.
help.exam: Short descriptive texts with colours, numbers and multiple-choice questions are a typical reading task at this level.
help.hook: One flag is older than eight hundred years, one is square, and one is called Black-Red-Gold. Read the stories of three flags.

quiz.passage:
Die Flagge von Deutschland hat drei Streifen: schwarz, rot und gold. Man sagt „Schwarz-Rot-Gold“. Die Farben sind alt, aber die Flagge ist jung: Sie ist die Flagge von Deutschland seit 1949. Gold ist hier eine Farbe, nicht gelb!

Die Flagge von Österreich hat auch drei Streifen: rot, weiß, rot. Sie ist eine der ältesten Flaggen der Welt. Die Geschichte sagt: Ein Herzog kämpft im Jahr 1191. Sein weißes Hemd wird rot von Blut. Nur der Gürtel in der Mitte bleibt weiß. Das ist die Flagge: rot, weiß, rot.

Die Flagge der Schweiz ist rot mit einem weißen Kreuz. Sie ist besonders: Sie ist quadratisch! Fast alle Flaggen der Welt sind Rechtecke. Nur zwei sind Quadrate: die Flagge der Schweiz und die Flagge des Vatikans. Und noch etwas: Das Rote Kreuz kommt aus der Schweiz. Sein Zeichen ist die Schweizer Flagge mit anderen Farben, ein rotes Kreuz auf weißem Grund.
quiz.passageTranslation:
The flag of Germany has three stripes: black, red and gold. People say 'Black-Red-Gold'. The colours are old, but the flag is young: it has been the flag of Germany since 1949. Gold is a colour here, not yellow!

The flag of Austria also has three stripes: red, white, red. It is one of the oldest flags in the world. The story says: a duke fights in the year 1191. His white shirt turns red with blood. Only the belt in the middle stays white. That is the flag: red, white, red.

The flag of Switzerland is red with a white cross. It is special: it is square! Almost all flags in the world are rectangles. Only two are squares: the flag of Switzerland and the flag of the Vatican. And one more thing: the Red Cross comes from Switzerland. Its sign is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped, a red cross on a white ground.

vocab.example: Der Markt ist jeden Sonntag offen.
Sie werfen die Bananen in eine Tüte.

quiz.title: Lesen: Sonntag, fünf Uhr, Fischmarkt

help.intro: A short text of about 130 words about the strangest market in Germany: the Hamburg fish market, which opens every Sunday at five in the morning, has done so since 1703, and where the sellers shout their prices and throw bananas and eels into bags. The facts are real and were checked. You need what you have just learnt: plural forms of food words (Fische, Bananen, Äpfel, Blumen), the articles in the nominative, numbers and prices (zehn Euro, fünf Uhr), and the question words Wann? (when), Was? (what), Wer? (who). Read for the gist first, then answer each question from one sentence of the text.

tips.title: Plurals at the market
tips.text: der Fisch → die Fische, der Apfel → die Äpfel, die Banane → die Bananen, die Blume → die Blumen, der Aal → die Aale, die Tüte → die Tüten, der Euro → stays Euro after a number (zehn Euro), die Uhr → fünf Uhr (time, no plural). Many feminine nouns take -n or -en; many masculine nouns take -e, and some change only the vowel (Äpfel).

examples.de: Zehn Bananen, fünf Äpfel und drei Fische in einer Tüte.
examples.en: Ten bananas, five apples and three fish in one bag.

examples.de: Die Tüte kostet nur zehn Euro!
examples.en: The bag costs only ten euros!

check.q: What is the plural of der Apfel?
check.why: Apfel takes an umlaut and no ending: Äpfel.

tips.title: Wann? Um wie viel Uhr?
tips.text: Wann? asks for a time or a day: am Sonntag, um fünf Uhr, seit 1703. Um fünf Uhr = at five o'clock; von fünf bis halb zehn = from five to half past nine (halb zehn is 9:30, half before ten!). Seit = since: seit 1703, seit dreihundert Jahren.

examples.de: Der Markt beginnt um fünf Uhr und endet um halb zehn.
examples.en: The market starts at five o'clock and ends at half past nine.

examples.de: Den Fischmarkt gibt es seit 1703.
examples.en: The fish market has existed since 1703.

check.why: halb zehn = half (on the way) to ten = 9:30. Careful: not half past ten.

remember: Plurals: Fische, Äpfel, Bananen, Blumen, Tüten; zehn Euro stays Euro.
um fünf Uhr = at five; halb zehn = 9:30; seit 1703 = since 1703.
help.exam: Short texts about markets, shopping and times with multiple-choice questions are a typical reading task at this level.
help.hook: Sunday, five in the morning, and thousands of people buy fish, bananas and flowers while the sellers shout. Read about Hamburg's wildest market.

quiz.passage:

help.intro: A phone call of about one and a half minutes: a guest books a hotel room in Konstanz and has to spell her name, her e-mail address and her street. The receptionist uses the German spelling alphabet, the one every German knows from the phone: A wie Anton, B wie Berta, C wie Cäsar, and so on. The scene is invented; the spelling words are the real ones used in Germany. You hear what you have just learnt: the letters of the alphabet, numbers in a phone number, and the questions Wie heißen Sie? Wie schreibt man das? Wie ist Ihre Telefonnummer? Listen once for the whole call, then once more for each spelled word.

tips.title: The German spelling alphabet
tips.text: On the phone Germans say a letter and a name: A wie Anton, B wie Berta, C wie Cäsar, D wie Dora, E wie Emil, F wie Friedrich, G wie Gustav, H wie Heinrich, I wie Ida, J wie Julius, K wie Kaufmann, L wie Ludwig, M wie Martha, N wie Nordpol, O wie Otto, P wie Paula, Q wie Quelle, R wie Richard, S wie Samuel (or Siegfried), T wie Theodor, U wie Ulrich, V wie Viktor, W wie Wilhelm, X wie Xanthippe, Y wie Ypsilon, Z wie Zacharias. Umlauts: Ä wie Ärger, Ö wie Ökonom, Ü wie Übermut; ß = Eszett or scharfes S.

quiz.title: Hören: Im Kaffeehaus

help.intro: A scene of about one and a half minutes in a Vienna coffee house: two friends order, and the waiter explains the famous Viennese coffee names, Melange, Einspänner, kleiner Brauner, which even Germans do not know. The scene is invented; the coffee names and the coffee-house customs are real, and since 2011 the Viennese coffee house is on the UNESCO list of cultural heritage. You hear what you have just learnt: sein and haben in all persons (ich bin, wir sind, haben Sie, ich habe), numbers and prices (vier Euro zwanzig), and the polite ich möchte / ich nehme. Listen once for the whole scene, then once for each order and each price.

tips.title: sein and haben at the table
tips.text: sein: ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind. haben: ich habe, du hast, er/sie hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben. In a café you hear: Haben Sie Tee? (Do you have tea?), Wir sind zu zweit (there are two of us), Ich habe Hunger (I am hungry: German has hunger), Das ist eine Melange (that is a Melange), Sind Sie fertig? (are you ready?).

tips.title: Vienna's coffee words
tips.text: Melange = coffee with frothed milk, the classic. Kleiner / großer Brauner = a small or large espresso with a little milk on the side. Einspänner = black coffee in a glass with a mountain of whipped cream (named after the one-horse carriage). Verlängerter = espresso with extra hot water. Every coffee comes with a glass of water on a silver tray. Prices: vier Euro zwanzig = 4.20; you say Euro and then the cents, no comma word.

check.why: The Melange is the classic Viennese coffee with milk foam; the Einspänner has whipped cream.

quiz.title: Hören: Wo ist mein Schlüssel?

help.intro: A scene of about one and a half minutes in a flat on a Monday morning: Jonas is late and cannot find his key, his phone, his glasses or his bag, and his flatmate Sara tells him where everything is. The scene is invented. You hear what you have just learnt: Wo ist …? with the answers in, auf, unter, neben, hinter, vor + the dative (auf dem Tisch, in der Küche, unter dem Sofa), and verbs with a vowel change (du siehst, er sieht, du nimmst, er isst). Listen once for the whole scene, then once per object: where is it in the end?

tips.title: Wo? + dative
tips.text: The question Wo? (where) gets an answer with a preposition and the dative: der Tisch → auf dem Tisch; das Sofa → unter dem Sofa; die Küche → in der Küche; die Tasche → in der Tasche. In short: der and das become dem, die becomes der. in dem is usually im: im Bad, im Kühlschrank. The prepositions: in (in), auf (on top of), unter (under), neben (next to), hinter (behind), vor (in front of), zwischen (between).

examples.de: Wo ist der Schlüssel? Er liegt auf dem Tisch, neben der Zeitung.
examples.en: Where is the key? It is lying on the table, next to the newspaper.

examples.de: Wo ist die Brille? Sie ist im Bad, vor dem Spiegel.
examples.en: Where are the glasses? They are in the bathroom, in front of the mirror.

check.q: Wo ist das Handy? Es ist ____ Sofa.
check.why: Wo? takes the dative; das Sofa → dem Sofa.

tips.title: Verbs that change their vowel
tips.text: Some verbs change e → ie / i or a → ä only for du and er/sie/es: sehen: ich sehe, du siehst, er sieht. nehmen: ich nehme, du nimmst, er nimmt. essen: ich esse, du isst, er isst. fahren: ich fahre, du fährst, er fährt. schlafen: du schläfst, er schläft. The wir, ihr and sie forms keep the normal vowel: wir sehen, ihr nehmt.

examples.de: Siehst du meine Brille? Nein, ich sehe sie nicht.
examples.en: Do you see my glasses? No, I do not see them.

examples.de: Du nimmst den Bus um acht, und er fährt um acht Uhr fünf.
examples.en: You take the bus at eight, and it leaves at five past eight.

check.why: essen changes e → i for du and er: er isst (spelled with ss since the reform).

du siehst / er sieht, du nimmst / er nimmt, du isst / er isst, er fährt.
